title: Blurry game when there is movement

posts.author: temp444
posts.body:
So I noticed that my events get blurry when there is camera movement.
If the player is stopped, all events look crispy and nice.
If the player moves but the map is small enough that the camera doesn't scroll, all events look crispy and nice.
If the player moves and the camera scrolls, events get a bit blurry.
If the player moves very fast (by dashing) and the camera scrolls, events get very blurry.
I thought it might be plugins or my resolution but I just created a new empty project at default resolution with 0 plugins, made a big map and placed a bunch of events around, and the issues above are all still true. It's also not a full screen issue since I'm testing this empty project on windowed mode.
I have seen other older posts mentioning this issue but the replies always said it was a resolution problem, yet this is still happening on a default resolution project like I tested above. It gets quite jarring when there's a lot of events on the screen, if you don't focus on the player sprite you could get dizzy
Posting here cus I've tested all kinds of anti blur and screen control plugins but can't seem to fix it
Thanks for reading!

posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
one of the biggest problem here is that there are several completely different effects that register as "blur" to the human eye, and each one has a different cause and solution.
That is the reason why it's always a gamble if a solution works or not - a zoom-blur needs a different solution than a motion-blur and so on.
And it is exetremely difficult to identify the correct cause of a blur through a text description on the internet, especially if the poster doesn't know what to look for.
here are a few question to help check the possibilities:
1) what is your game screen size?
2) what is your windows/monitor screen size?
3) what is your fps?

posts.author: TheAM-Dol
posts.body:
See, my first thought of "blurriness when in motion" would be your monitors pixel-to-pixel time. That is, the amount of time it takes for the pixels in your monitor to change to a different color. (I think sometimes called grey-to-grey)
Older, cheaper, or older and cheaper monitors may have blur due to the cheap panel.
It's less noticeable when moving "through" the scene (such as in a first person perspective", but often lateral movement makes pixel-to-pixel pretty obvious.
You can test response time here:
Blur Busters TestUFO Motion Tests. Benchmark for monitors & displays.
Blur Busters UFO Motion Tests with ghosting test, 30fps vs 60fps vs 120hz vs 144hz vs 240hz, PWM test, motion blur test, judder test, benchmarks, and more.

posts.author: TheAM-Dol
posts.body:
Lol, sending screenshot of a motion blur test is pointless. The images are all rendered at full sharpness. If they look soft at all when viewing then from the website, then it's your monitor. The motion blur isn't generated by the website. So a screen shot is going to look sharp no matter what.
The video looks sharp to me. I watched it on my phone, a flagship device with a top-tier screen. Aliens look sharper on my phone than my home monitor and my home monitor has great pixel response time. So that being said: your video looks sharp as a tack.
If you want to verify if it's your monitor or generated by the engine, try recording a video and slowing it down.
Ideally, you would record at the same frame rate as the game to avoid frame interpolation. However, most software doesn't allow 144hz capture, so next best thing is capping the frame rate of the game to 60 and recording it at 60fps. Then take the footage and slow it down. If you see blurry pixels in the footage, it's the engine, if it looks sharp (or sharper) slowed down, it's your hardware.
Actually a thought that just popped into my head while writing this: while moving left or right, take a screen shot when you see the blur. Is the blur in the screen shot or is it gone?

posts.author: TheAM-Dol
posts.body:
raffle said:
it's actually a refresh rate or vsync thing going on here?
Click to expand...
No, neither.
Typically refresh rate is used to describe the rate at which your monitor can accept a new frame. Most computer monitors run at 60hz or in other words can accept a new frame of data 60 times every second. It seems you are using a 144hz monitor, so it can accept a new frame of data 144 times every second. However, just because it is accepting the frame data to draw the image, the individual pixels need to light up to
display
that image. Pixels can light up seemingly near instantly, but maybe have just a few milliseconds of delay before they reach peak brightness. If those "few milliseconds" are longer than the time it takes for your monitor to draw a new frame, the pixels brightness will overlap the next frame and will result in blurring of the image because the pixels from the previous frame are still being lit up when a new frame is being drawn. The result is what appears to be something akin to motion blur or "ghosting".
This article
will talk about these properties of monitors and clarify some points. But the key take away concerning your situation would be this:
Why Response Time Is Important​
If you are a casual internet user, meaning you simply browse, shop, or read, response time is not really an important factor. In fact, even if you regularly use your PC for things like watching movies or videos, response time still may not be that big of a deal for you.
If you are a videographer, or even more so, a gamer, response time matters quite a lot. Having a lower response rate, such as one to five milliseconds can make all the difference for you. It also allows for more distinct motion and less of what is called
“ghosting”
.
Click to expand...
(keep in mind this article is written by ViewSonic who is a manufacturer of computer displays, so there will be an inherit bias if they discuss any products.)
So basically: It's not really anything you should worry about. It's likely not worth the investment in a new monitor just to make it go away. You could try down-clocking your monitor's refresh rate (I believe this is accessible via the Nvidia control panel). 120hz may reduce the ghosting since that will allow slightly more time between frames for the pixels to adjust.
But, it's hardly worth rushing out to fix. Though, not gonna lie, upgrading to at least a 1440p monitor makes such a huge difference (and 4k in gaming is still so difficult to drive, especially with a 10-series card - so 1440p is a good sweet spot of quality that is easier to drive), so maybe something to put on the Christmas list.
*side note, unrelated, you may, at some point, begin to experience a graphical crash when play testing your MV game because you are running on a high refresh rate monitor. So the link in my signature has a fix for that.

posts.author: TheAM-Dol
posts.body:
RM has a lot of rendering quirks. Not so long ago (and still on going) we were trying to diagnose
this users problem
which also seems to be a rendering quirk of the engine.
The fact of the matter is that...well, it's kind of the nature of the engine. I don't mean to downplay yours or anyone else's problems with the rendering, but at the same time, this isn't exactly Unreal with high fidelity graphics, it's not even Godot - heck, it's not even Game Maker. All of which have more robust rendering pipelines than RPG Maker.
RPG Maker isn't about robust renderers. It's about being a light-weight RPG Making tool that can run on browsers and mobile devices, so naturally the render pipeline just isn't the priority of the devs of the engine. So we wind up with some frame-pacing issues, some soft pixels, fixed internal render resolutions.
In the scheme of things, these render quirks are not what you should be concerned about when delivering a game. I would be more concerned about making a good game first. Some soft "motion blur" is probably not going to kill your game for your potential customers.
If your game becomes successful to the point where you start having a handful of people complain about the problem, then with the success of your game you could consider commissioning a fix with all that cash you are raking in. But let's just focus on getting the game out first.

posts.author: MeowthurMorgan
posts.body:
So I actually have a weird and not a very efficient solution for this particular issue. I'll explain why I said that in a bit. But rest assured it fixes the issue.
First I'll explain how and when if faced this problem. (Cuz i need a better solution sometimes)
I have a 1080p monitor with a 5600x and 3070, which is perfectly capable of playing RDR2 in 1080p, which I was until i noticed this weird issue, when i move the textures seem shimmery and blurry, especially around the vegetation, but it completely fixes when i stop moving the camera.
So my watch began. Did everything I found online tried every setting, until I found a weird solution.
[Solution]
I went to nvidia control panel, looked up DSR, turned 4k and 2k DSR on, that allowed my windows to render games at 4k too.
So after doing that, even if you run windows at 1080p you can play games at 4k using exclusive fullscreen, which I did, and finally only running the game at 4k completely fixed the issue at the cost of a solid chunk of performance. Not even 2k fixed the issue. Well i still could run the game at 4k 60 using dlss balanced and the visuals became out-freakin-standing but yeah not every game is as optimized as RDR2.
Same problem occured for Witcher 3 and Cyberpunk. Same Solution. (yeah i used frame gen mods in both which looks fkin fine tbh}.
P.S. Cyberpunk actually got fixed at 2k tho lol.
And please if anyone gets a fix that doesnt require a huge performance expense, do tell me.

It's a bit of a fallacy to compare RPG Maker games to...well any other game.
The engine itself under utilizes hardware. MV games in particular are notorious for utilizing the GPU practically 0% of the time. Meaningwhile, MZ is somewhat better at utilizing the GPU, but still a bulk of it's processing is handled by the CPU.
Even then, the CPU at best only has a couple of cores/threads being utilized.
As I mentioned last year:
TheAM-Dol said:
RPG Maker isn't about robust renderers. It's about being a light-weight RPG Making tool that can run on browsers and mobile devices
Click to expand...
Secondly, what I suspect you are experiencing is either a driver problem or it could even be your monitor, as each monitor has a "pixel response time" which is basically how quickly a pixel can turn off/change color. Particularly low quality monitors can have pretty bad pixel response time which can show up as smearing.
You can test your monitor here:
Blur Busters TestUFO Motion Tests. Benchmark for monitors & displays.
Blur Busters UFO Motion Tests with ghosting test, 30fps vs 60fps vs 120hz vs 144hz vs 240hz, PWM test, motion blur test, judder test, benchmarks, and more.
www.testufo.com
Some forms of TAA and/or AI Frame Generation can result in smeary frames in 3D games. If the game offers better AA solutions, I recommend using them over TAA; though, unfortunately, many newer games require TAA as part of their render pipeline in order to "refine" the image.
That's an entirely different topic related to this subject, so I'll leave it up to you to research it.
